div.p: For mixed-criticality (MC) systems, recent studies show that it can be important to provide continuous (albeit degraded) services for low-critical (LC) tasks even in the high running mode. In this paper, focusing on dual-criticality systems, we study a mode-switch fixed-priority (MS-FP) scheduler for a set of dual-rate mixed-criticality (DR-MC) tasks, where each LC task can have a pair of small and large periods to represent its service requirements in the low (LO) and high (HI) running modes, respectively. Moreover, DR-MC tasks may adjust their priorities at the mode-switch point for better system schedulability. By extending the response time analysis (RTA) technique for MC systems, we first derive the schedulability conditions for a set of DR-MC tasks under the MS-FP scheduler with mode transition being considered. Then, we investigate how to select periods and priorities of DR-MC tasks to optimize their control performance and formulate it as a Non-Linear Optimization problem. We propose an efficient heuristic for a simplified optimization problem based on Branch & Bound Search Tree (BBST) technique. The effectiveness of the proposed heuristic and the MS-FP scheduler with DR-MC task model is illustrated through one case study with four tasks and compared against the Ipopt solutions.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recently, mixed-criticality (MC) systems have become the subject of an important research area considering the advancement of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). In those systems, real-time control tasks can have different criticality levels depending on their functionalities. For instance, in avionic industry, it is typically more important to guarantee flightcritical (e.g., flight-control) tasks than mission-oriented tasks (e.g., capturing photos) [3]. In general, the tasks of those systems are certified by different authorities with different levels of pessimism, which results in quite different worstcase execution time (WCET) estimations.

In the seminal work [27], Vestal considered that a MC system starts at the low (LO) running mode assuming that tasks take their low-level (i.e., smaller) WCETs. At runtime, whenever a high-critical task takes more time than its lowlevel WCET, the system will switch to the high (HI) running mode where all low-critical tasks will be discarded to provide the extra computation capacity demanded by high-critical tasks. Following this work, many mixed-criticality scheduling algorithms have been developed considering various system This work was supported in part by US NSF CAREER Award CNS-0953005 and grant CNS-1422709. models and scheduling policies in the last few years [4], [8], [19], [14], [26], [29]. A comprehensive review of these algorithms can be found in [12].

For fixed-priority scheduling, Baruah et al. studied a novel response-time analysis (RTA) technique for mixed-criticality systems with mode transition being considered [6]. Moreover, to further improve system schedulability ratio, the same authors investigated a priority re-ordering scheme for highcritical tasks after the mode transition [7], where the mixedcriticality task system was transformed into a regular sporadic task system with release-jitters. In [5], Baruah and Burns further explored a period transformation technique when scheduling mixed-criticality tasks in order to improve utilization efficiency by constructing harmonic periods. However, as in most other mixed-criticality scheduling work, the above studies [5], [6] discarded low-critical tasks at the mode transition point to ensure the timeliness of high-critical tasks.

Note that, due to the possible runtime cancellation, the execution of low-critical tasks in most existing MC scheduling algorithms is rather intermittent. That is, to accommodate the high-level WCETs of high-critical tasks, the low-critical tasks will be discarded immediately to release their computation capacity whenever any high-critical task overruns (i.e., uses more time than its low-level WCET) and causes a running mode switch [4], [6], [7], [19], [27].

Although such a cancellation approach is effective to provide guaranteed executions for high-critical tasks, it can severely degrade the service levels for low-critical tasks and may not even be acceptable for some applications [16]. In realtime control systems, the performance of control tasks and system stability are normally represented by the performance loss index (PLI), which depends directly on the service intervals (i.e., periods) and delays (i.e., worst-case response time) of control tasks [9], [22], [23], [28]. In a recent study [11], Burns and Baruah highlighted the fact that, to maintain the stability of a real-time control system, it can be vital to allow LC tasks to make some progress rather than completely abandoning them after the system enters the HI running mode.

Therefore, to mitigate the effects of cancellation on lowcritical tasks in MC systems, a few studies have investigated schemes to delay the cancellation without sacrificing system's schedulability [15], [20]. Moreover, the mechanism of determining when and how to switch the system back to the LO running mode for resuming the execution of lowcritical tasks is further discussed in [21]. However, those (delayed cancellation or early resumption) approaches still cannot provide any guaranteed services for low-critical tasks in the HI running mode.

As the first attempt to provide guaranteed services for lowcritical tasks, following the ideas of elastic scheduling [13], we have studied the Elastic Mixed-Critical (E-MC) task model [25]. The basic idea is to allow each low-critical task to have a maximum period that defines its minimum service level, which is guaranteed offline even with the high-level WCETs of all high-critical tasks being considered. The work was extended to multicore systems based on partitioned scheduling in [26]. In [24], we further studied a dual-rate mixed-criticality (DR-MC) task model where a low-critical task can have a pair of periods to represent its service requirements in the low (LO) and high (HI) running modes, respectively. Focusing on dynamic priority EDF scheduling, we studied the schedulability condition and investigated the trade-offs between the service guarantees (i.e., the small and large periods) of low-critical tasks in different running modes.

However, to the best of our knowledge, there is very limited work on guaranteeing the service requirements for lowcritical tasks under fixed-priority scheduling. In [11], Burns and Baruah emphasized a few guidelines to handle lowcritical tasks when a MC system switches from LO to HI running modes: 1) reduce the priorities of low-critical tasks; 2) reduce the execution budgets for low-critical tasks; 3) increase the periods (i.e., service intervals) of low-critical tasks. The authors discussed the second approach in details without much elaboration on the first and the third options [11].

Inspired by the above guidelines and based on our previous work, we study a mode-switch fixed-priority (MS-FP) scheduler for dual-criticality systems. For a set of DR-MC tasks, we first derive the schedulability condition under the MS-FP scheduler by extending the response-time analysis (RTA) technique. Then, we formulate the control performance optimization problem for DR-MC tasks by selecting their periods/priorities as a Non-Linear Optimization problem and propose an efficient heuristic based on Branch & Bound Search Tree technique for a simplified problem. In summary, the contributions of this work are listed as follows:

• We introduce the MS-FP scheduler for DR-MC tasks, where a DR-MC task can have different periods (i.e., rates) and priorities in the LO and HI running modes; • By extending the RTA in [6], [11], we derive the schedulability condition for DR-MC tasks under MS-FP; • We formulate the control performance optimization problem for DR-MC tasks as a non-linear problem and propose an efficient heuristic solution based on the Branch & Bound Search Tree (BBST) technique; • We illustrate the effectiveness of the DR-MC model and proposed schemes through a case study. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The system models and the mode-switch fixed-priority (MS-FP) scheduling are presented in Section II. Section III discusses the extended RTA and presents the schedulability condition for DR-MC tasks under MS-FP. The control performance optimization problem for DR-MC tasks is formulated and an efficient heuristic solution is proposed in Section IV. Section V presents a case study and Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODELS AND PRELIMINARIES
div.p: With the focus on dual-criticality systems, we assume that there are two different running modes, which are indicated as low (LO) and high (HI), respectively. We consider a set of n tasks Γ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } to be executed on a single processor system, where the tasks are independent and do not share resources other than the processor.

div.head: A. Dual-Rate Mixed-Criticality (DR-MC) Task Model
div.p: Similar to the task model in [24], a DR-MC task τ i (i = 1, . . . , n) is characterized by a four-tuple of parameters:
div.formula: (ζ i , C i , P i , η i ). Here, ζ i denotes the criticality level of task τ i . That is, if τ i is a low-critical (LC) task, there is ζ i = LO;
div.p: otherwise, for a high-critical (HC) task τ i , we have ζ i = HI.

The vector C i = (c LO i , c HI i ) specifies the worst-case execution times (WCETs) of task τ i in the LO and HI running modes, respectively. Note that, the same as in the conventional MC model [27], for a LC task (i.e., ζ i = LO), we assume that its WCETs are equal (i.e., c LO i = c HI i ). Moreover, for a HC task (i.e., ζ i = HI), it is assumed that c LO i ≤ c HI i . Similarly, the vector P i = (p LO i , p HI i ) represents the periods (i.e., service intervals) of task τ i in the LO and HI running modes, respectively. Here, to guarantee the same executions of HC tasks as in the conventional MC systems, we assume that p LO i = p HI i for a HC task τ i . Moreover, to model the degraded service requirement of a LC task τ i , we assume that p LO i < p HI i . With the increased periods for LC tasks in the HI running mode, it is expected that their computation demands will decrease, which can provide the much needed extra capacity for HC tasks [24]. We consider task systems with implicit deadlines. That is, (p LO i , p HI i ) also represent the relative deadlines (d LO i , d HI i ) of task τ i in the LO and HI running modes, respectively.

To improve the schedulability of tasks, we assume that a DR-MC task τ i can have different priorities in the LO and HI running modes, which are denoted by the vector η i = (η LO i , η HI i ). η * i η * j indicates that task τ i has higher priority than that of task τ j in the '*' running mode, where '*' can be either LO or HI. Since tasks can have different priorities in different running modes, it is possible to have
div.formula: η LO i η LO j but η HI j η HI i .
div.p: Based on the priorities of the tasks, we define:
div.formula: hp * (i) = {τ k |τ k ∈ Γ ∧ η * k η * i } (1)
div.p: as the sets of DR-MC tasks with higher priorities than that of task τ i in the '*' running modes, respectively. Note that hp HI (i) can be different from hp LO (i) for a task τ i .

div.head: B. Mode-Switch Fixed-Priority (MS-FP) Execution Model
div.p: The above DR-MC task model has two aspects aiming at improving system schedulability in the HI running mode: the increased periods (i.e., service intervals) for LC tasks and adjusted priorities for all tasks. To incorporate those features of DR-MC tasks and following the ideas of the mode-switch EDF scheduler [16], [24], we consider the mode-switch fixedpriority (MS-FP) scheduling algorithm in this work, where the basic execution rules are defined as follows:

• Rule 1 [Initialization]: The system starts with the LO (i.e., normal) running mode; • Rule 2 [Normal Execution]: In the normal (LO) running mode, a DR-MC task τ i releases its jobs according to its low-level period p LO i . Its j th job, denoted by J j i , is released at time r j i with an absolute deadline r j i + p LO i . Its active job competes the processor with other active jobs using its low-level priority η LO i , where the processor always picks up the highest priority job for execution;

• Rule 3 [Overrun of LC Tasks]: The overrun of LC tasks is prohibited (in both LO and HI running modes); that is, for any LC job J j i (i.e., ζ i = LO), if it does not issue the completion signal after using up its WCET (c LO i = c HI i ), the job will be terminated immediately; • Rule 4 [Transition to HI]: When a HC job J j i (where ζ i = HI) does not signal completion after using up its low-level WCET (c LO i ), the system running mode switches from LO to HI at the moment of overrun (denoted by t * ); At that time, all active jobs also change their priorities from η LO to η HI . Thus, only active jobs of tasks from hp HI (i) can preempt job J j i after time t * . Moreover, for active LC jobs, their absolute deadlines are extended by (p HIp LO ); • Rule 5 [Urgent Execution]: In the HI (urgent) running mode, each DR-MC task τ i releases its jobs according to their high-level period p HI i (recall that, if τ i is a HC task, there is p HI i = p LO i ) and the active jobs compete the processor with their high-level priorities η HI . A system error occurs if a HC job J j i does not signal completion after using up its high-level WCET (c HI i ); • Rule 6 [Transition to LO]: We assume that the system switches back from the HI to LO running mode when it becomes idle [6]; after that, tasks will release and run according to Rule 2. Note that, it may be possible for the system to get back to the LO running mode early [16]; however, exploring this possibility is beyond the scope of this paper and will be left for our future work.

From the above execution rules of the MS-FP scheduler, we can see that HC tasks have the same guaranteed executions as in the existing fixed-priority scheduling [6] under both LO and HI running modes. However, MS-FP differs from existing work by allowing LC tasks to continue their executions (albeit with degraded services) under HI running mode. The schedulability of DR-MC tasks under MS-FP is defined as: Definition 1. For a set of DR-MC tasks that are scheduled under the MS-FP scheduler, if there is no deadline miss for any execution of the tasks under any circumstance (for both LO and HI running modes) provided that LC and HC tasks do not take more time than their c LO and c HI , respectively, the task set is said to be schedulable under MS-FP.

div.head: III. RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS (RTA) FOR DR-MC TASKS UNDER MS-FP
div.p: In this section, for a set of DR-MC tasks with known periods and priorities, we first formally analyze their schedulability under MS-FP by extending the worse-case response time analysis (RTA) in [6]. The problem of period selection and priority assignment for DR-MC tasks to optimize their control performance will be addressed in Section IV.

In what follows, the RTA for DR-MC tasks in the LO running mode is first derived in Section III-A. Then, with the mode transition being considered, the RTA for both LC and HC tasks are analyzed in Section III-B.

div.head: A. RTA for DR-MC Tasks in LO Running Mode
div.p: Note that, when the system operates in the LO running mode, no tasks take more time than their low-level WCET c LO . Moreover, both LC and HC tasks release their jobs regularly according to their low-level period p LO and are executed with their low-level (fixed) priorities η LO . Therefore, following the standard RTA approach, the worst-case response time R LO i for any (either LC or HI) task τ i in the LO running mode can be obtained iteratively as follows [6]:
div.formula: R LO i = c LO i + τj ∈hp LO (i) R LO i p LO j • c LO j (2)
div.p: Here, hp LO (i) is the set of tasks with higher priorities than that of task τ i in the LO running mode. Once the worst-case response times for all tasks are obtained, the schedulability of the DR-MC tasks in the LO running mode can be easily determined as stated in the following lemma.

Lemma 1. For a given set of DR-MC tasks to be scheduled under the MS-FP scheduler, if there is R LO i ≤ p LO i (i.e., its worst-case response time is no more than its low-level period) for every tasks τ i (i = 1, . . . , n), the task set is said to be schedulable in the LO running mode.

div.head: B. RTA for DR-MC Tasks in HI Running Mode
div.p: When any HC task τ i has an execution overrun (i.e., takes more time than its low-level WCET c LO i ), the moment of overrun is denoted as the mode transition time point t * . At that time, the system enters the HI running mode. Different from the existing work on fixed-priority mixed-criticality scheduling where LC tasks are discarded immediately [6], in this work, both HC and LC tasks can continue their executions after the mode transition under the MS-FP scheduler. Here, to improve system schedulability in the HI running mode, LC tasks will have increased periods (i.e., reduced execution rates) and all DR-MC tasks may need to adjust their priorities.

To incorporate the effects of mode transition, it is known that there are two types (i.e., crossing and normal) of jobs for HC tasks that need to be considered for analyzing their schedulability [6], [14]. In this work, both HC and LC tasks can continue their executions after the mode transition time point t * under the MS-FP scheduler. Therefore, we extend the definitions of crossing and normal jobs [16], [24] • Crossing jobs: both HC and LC active jobs that are released before but have their absolute deadlines after the mode transition time point t * ; • Normal jobs: both HC and LC jobs that are released after the mode transition time point t * ; The timing relationships for jobs at the mode switch point t * are illustrated in Figure 1. As shown in the figure, the deadline of a crossing HC job remains unchanged. Moreover, as there is p HI j = p LO j for a HC task τ j , its jobs are released in the HI running mode at the same rate as that in the LO running mode. In comparison, for a LC task τ i , its crossing job will have extended deadline (see Rule 4 in Section II-B) and its normal jobs in the HI running mode are released according to its increased high-level period p HI i .

Static RTA for Normal Jobs in HI Running Mode: Once all crossing jobs complete their executions, the system enters the stable HI running mode where only normal jobs of DR-MC tasks exist. Here, for the normal jobs (denoted by N) of a HC or LC task τ i in the stable HI running mode, we can apply the static analysis [6] and obtain the response time R HI i (N) (which does not consider crossing jobs) as:
div.formula: R HI i (N) = c HI i + τj ∈hp HI (i) R HI i (N) p HI j c HI j (3)
div.p: Recall that, hp HI (i) refers to the set of tasks with priority higher than that of task τ i in the HI running mode. However, as shown later in Theorem 1, R HI i (N) calculated from the above equation is dominated by the one that considered crossing jobs, which will be discussed below.

RTA with Crossing Jobs being Considered: Suppose that the crossing job of a task τ i was released at r i (see Figure 1). If there were r i + R LO i < t * (i.e., the mode transition happens after its worst-case response time in the LO running mode), it indicates that the crossing job of τ i should have completed its execution before time t * , which contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have t * ≤ r i +R LO i and it is possible that the mode transition happens before τ i 's crossing job completes its execution. Here, the execution of τ i 's crossing job can span across t * . Recall that, tasks may change their priorities at time t * . Therefore, the execution of τ i 's crossing job can be interfered by tasks in both hp LO (i) and hp HI (i).

To derive the worst-case response time for the crossing job of task τ i , which is denoted by R HI i (C), we first analyze the interference from high priority tasks in both LO and HI running modes. Note that, the high priority tasks can be either LC or HC tasks, which have different interferences with the execution of task τ i 's crossing job. Therefore, to categorize those high priority tasks, we define the following notations:

div.head: C. A Motivational Example
div.p: To illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed DR-MC task model and the MS-FP scheduler on providing graceful service degradation for LC tasks and improving system schedulability, we consider an example set of three tasks Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 }. Here, the first task τ 1 is a LC task while the other two (τ 2 and τ 3 ) are HC tasks. The timing parameters for the tasks are shown in Table I.

For comparison, we start with the timing parameters for the tasks in the MC model [6]. Here, for the LC task τ 1 , the p MC i denotes its desired period (i.e., service interval). Suppose that the tasks are prioritized in the order of (τ 1 τ 2 τ 3 ).

Task To determine the schedulability of the MC tasks under fixedpriority scheduling, a simple and intuitive approach is to transform them into classical real-time tasks through worstcase reservation (WCR). Basically, the high-level WCETs for HC tasks (i.e., 5 for τ 2 and 22 for τ 3 ) are reserved as shown in the last column in Table I, where the classical RTA can be performed on the tasks. However, as shown in Table II, we can see that the task set is deemed as unschedulable under WCR as there is R 3 > p 3 . Next, we consider the adaptive mixed-criticality scheduling scheme (denoted as AMC-rtb), which was proposed in [6]. In the LO running mode, as shown in Table II, we can see that the worst-case response time for all tasks is no more than their periods. However, once the system enters the HI running mode, AMC-rtb discards the LC task τ 1 to ensure the executions of HC tasks (τ 2 and τ 3 ) in the HI running mode. With the mode transient being considered, we can find that the worst-case responses times for tasks τ 2 and τ 3 in the HI running mode are 6 and 69, respectively. Therefore, the task set is schedulable under AMC-rtb [6].

div.p: Note that, the cancellation of the LC task τ 1 in the HI running mode under AMC-rtb [6] may cause serious service interruption, especially for control systems. To enable the graceful service degradation for the LC task τ 1 , a larger period p HI 1 = 28 is considered for task τ 1 in the HI running mode in our DR-MC model. That is, instead of being completely discarded, task τ 1 can increase its period from p LO i = 4 (its desired period) to p HI i = 28 when the system enters the HI running mode. For the HC tasks τ 2 and τ 3 , as shown in Table I, their service intervals (i.e., periods) remain unchanged. Moreover, to ensure the schedulability of the tasks in the HI running mode, the priorities of tasks need to be adjusted as (τ 2 τ 1 τ 3 ) at the mode transition time point.

Based on the RTA analysis, the worst-case response times for the tasks with the DR-MC model under the MS-FP scheduler can be found as shown in Table II. Here, we can see that the tasks have the same worst-case response times in the LO running mode as those under AMC-rtb. However, in the HI running mode, with the increased period for the LC task τ 1 and adjusted priorities of the tasks, the worst-case response times for all tasks under MS-FP are no more than their respective periods. Therefore, according to Lemma 2, the task set with DR-MC parameters is schedulable under MS-FP.

From this example, we can see that, with the DR-MC task model and MS-FP scheduler, it is possible to provide gracefully degraded services for LC tasks (by having larger periods) in the HI running mode without sacrificing the timeliness of HC tasks. Moreover, the priorities of both HC and LC tasks may change to ensure their schedulability.

div.head: IV. CONTROL PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION
div.p: The schedulability condition for a set of DR-MC tasks with known/fixed periods and priorities under the MS-FP scheduler was analyzed in the previous section. Next, we investigate the problem of appropriately selecting the periods and priorities for DR-MC tasks with the objective to optimize their control performance while ensuring their schedulability.

Intuitively, having larger periods and lower priorities for LC tasks in the HI running mode can provide better opportunities to serve HC tasks and improve system schedulability after a running mode switch. However, it also means much degraded services with increased service intervals and response times for LC tasks. Note that, in real-time control systems, the control performance of a task is usually presented as its performance loss index (PLI) [22], [23], [28].
For a task τ i , its P LI i can be approximated as a linear function of its period (p i ) and feedback latency (R i ; i.e., its worst-case response time) [9]:
div.formula: P LI i ≈ a i • p i + b i • R i (17)
div.p: where (a i , b i ) is a pair of positive coefficient factors that indicate the weights of the period and latency of task τ i on its control performance. In general, larger values of P LI indicate worse control performance [9].

div.head: A. Control Optimization Problems for DR-MC Tasks
div.p: With both LO and HI running modes being considered, the overall system control performance for a set Γ of DR-MC tasks can be represented as:
div.formula: P LI DRMC = τi∈Γ (x i • P LI LO i + y i • P LI HI i ) (18) P LI LO i = a LO i • p LO i + b LO i • R LO i (19) P LI HI i = a HI i • p HI i + b HI i • R HI i (20)
div.p: where x i and y i indicate the weight of task τ i 's control performance in LO and HI running modes, respectively, on the overall system. The above formulation provides flexibility for system designers to weight tasks and optimize system performance in different running modes. However, considering the fact that it is rather a rare event for a system entering the HI running mode and the system runs in the LO (normal) mode for the majority of the time, in this work, we focus on the control performance for tasks in the LO running mode and set x i = 1 and y i = 0 (i = 1, . . . , n) accordingly.

To comply with the basic principle of mixed-criticality systems, we assume that the executions of HC tasks are guaranteed in both LO and HI running modes [6] (i.e., their timing parameters, including WCETs and periods, are pre-fixed and cannot be changed). Moreover, the period of a control task τ i normally needs to be within a range [p min i , p max i ], which are determined by the physical plant to be controlled and/or system configurations [22], [23], [28].

The DRMC-Opt Problem: The general problem of control performance optimization for DR-MC tasks can be informally described as: for a set of DR-MC tasks where C i for all tasks, P i for HC tasks and (p min i , p max i ) for LC tasks are given, finding the periods (p LO , p HI ) of LC tasks and the priorities of all tasks in both LO and HI running modes with the objective to minimize P LI DRMC , subject to the conditions that: a). the periods of LC tasks are in their respective ranges; and b). the tasks are schedulable under the MS-FP scheduler.

From discussions in the last section, we can see that even a small adjustment for the periods and/or priorities of the tasks can have very complicated impacts on their worst-case response times in the HI running mode (especially with the crossing jobs being considered). On the other hand, the system operates in the normal (LO) running mode for majority of the time and the probability of the system entering the HI running mode is rather small. Therefore, to simplify the optimization problem as well as to increase the chance of finding a feasible solution, for the rest of the paper, we consider the case where there is p HI i = p max i for each LC task τ i .

div.p: Note that, the above formulation can easily adapt to various situations through the adjustment of co-efficient (a * i and b * i ) and weight (x i and y i ) factors. For instance, if task τ i is a feedback-sensitive control task, its P LI can benefit (or suffer) more from feedback latency compared with control period [17]. In this case, we can assign b * i relatively large values compared to those of a * i . Moreover, if some (especially HC) tasks have great impacts on the stability of the system, we can increase their weight factors to get a solution that favor these tasks. Once these factors are determined by system engineers, a generic non-linear optimization solver such as Ipopt [1] can be deployed to optimally solve the problem.

div.head: C. A Branch & Bound Search Tree (BBST) Based Heuristic
div.p: Note that, once the low-level periods of LC tasks are determined, to find out whether there exists a feasible priority assignment for a set of n DR-MC tasks, we need to check n! • n! possible priority assignments as there are n! priority assignments for the tasks in both LO and HI running modes. Therefore, the complexity for solving the above non-linear problem can be quite high, especially for systems with a large number of tasks. Hence, to further simplify the optimization problem, instead of allowing each LC task τ i to choose its low-level period p LO i independently, we can define a scaling factor β and enforce all LC tasks to adjust their low-level periods uniformly. The heuristic starts with the low-level priority assignment for the tasks. To avoid inspecting all n! possible assignments of η LO for the tasks, it adopts the recursive Branch & Bound Search Tree (BBST) technique [18] to effectively prune the infeasible and/or inefficient (partial) priority assignments. The high-level structure of the BBST-based heuristic is as follows: the scheme starts with Γ s = ∅ and the highest priority as the next available priority. It adds one task at a time to Γ s and assigns its low-level priority as the next available priority. That is, the first added task has the highest low-level priority while the last one has the lowest low-level priority so far.
For each Branch & Bound operation, it checks whether this subset Γ s (⊆ Γ) of tasks with their assigned low-level priorities can potentially lead to a feasible and better solution.

If not, it indicates that it is impossible to get the solution with the partial low-level priority assignment for the tasks in Γ s , which can be pruned without further consideration. Otherwise, a new task (if any) will be added to Γ s with its low-level priority being properly assigned. When all tasks are in Γ s and the corresponding low-level priority assignment can lead to a valid β and a schedulable high-level priority assignment for the tasks, a feasible solution is found. From all feasible solutions, we can get the value of β and the priority assignments of tasks that result in the smallest P LI DRMC . BBST-Heuristic Prune Decisions: The key factor for the efficiency of the BBST-based heuristic is to prune an infeasible and/or inefficient partial priority assignment as early as possible. Without loss of generality, suppose that

First, based on the results in [10], we can find the intervals for β (if exist) such that the tasks in Γ s are schedulable in the LO running mode (line 3). Then, for each interval of β obtained above, the minimum β (which can result in the smallest P LI i , i = 1, . . . , k) and the corresponding feasible (if exists) high-level priority assignment θ HI (Γ s ) for the tasks in Γ s can be obtained with Audsley's OPA algorithm [2].

Find Feasible β Intervals for LC Tasks: Here, we focus on the schedulability of tasks in Γ s in the LO running mode. That is, we try to find intervals for β such that the resulting low-level periods for LC tasks from any value of β in these intervals will ensure the schedulability of the tasks in the LO running mode. For such a purpose, we exploit the results in [10], which can be rephrased as follows: Lemma 3. For a set of n real-time tasks with given fixed priorities, WCETs and the ranges of their periods, if there exist feasible periods of the tasks to ensure their schedulability under the fixed priority scheduling, they can be represented as m(≥ 1) sets of period ranges for the tasks:

div.p: Basically, it says that, if every task τ i takes any period from its range [p LB i,x , p UB i,x ] in P x , the task set is schedulable under fixed priority scheduling. From another point of view, the period ranges in P x actually define a certain relation between tasks' periods (corresponding to the ceiling operations in the RTA for fixed priority scheduling). That is, when periods of tasks vary within their ranges in P x , the relation between tasks' periods are kept the same and the response times of the tasks remain unchanged [10].

Hence, for the tasks in Γ s , we can get its solutions as . If the intersection of these intervals is not empty, a common interval [β LB x , β UB x ] for all LC tasks can be found for P x . Otherwise, there is no feasible β for P x .

Here, if there exists at least one feasible interval for β from {P 1 , • • • , P m }, it means that we can have feasible low-level period assignments for LC tasks (i.e., β) to make Γ s schedulable in the LO running mode. Otherwise, Γ s cannot lead to a feasible solution and should be pruned.

High-Level Priority Assignment for All Tasks: Suppose that the set of feasible intervals for β found in the last steps is {[β LB x , β UB x ]|x = 1, . . . , m}. For a given value of β within one of its feasible intervals, the periods of LC tasks become fixed. Next, we need to find the corresponding high-level priority assignment θ HI (Γ s ) for tasks in Γ s that can ensure their schedulability in the HI running mode.

Here, based on the RTA discussed in the last section, we can get that the schedulability test for the tasks in the HI running mode satisfies the three conditions of Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA) algorithm for fixed priority tasks [2]. Therefore, the feasible (if exists) high-level priority assignment θ HI (Γ s ) to ensure their schedulability in the HI running mode can be efficiently obtained with the OPA algorithm [2].

From above discussions, when β varies within one of its feasible intervals, the worst-case response times for the tasks in Γ s in the LO running mode remain unchanged [10]. However, the low-level periods for LC tasks increase monotonically with larger values of β. Therefore, to obtain the smallest P LI DRMC , it is desired for β to take the lower bound of each feasible interval. However, such a choice of β may lead to infeasible high-level priority assignment for the tasks. Hence, for each feasible interval of β, the smallest β that enables a feasible high-level priority assignment for the tasks can be found through binary search.

If it turns out that, within all the feasible intervals, there does not exist a value of β that can lead to feasible high-level priority assignment for the tasks, it indicates that Γ s can not lead to a feasible solution and should be pruned. Otherwise, at least one feasible pair of β and high-level priority assignment for the tasks θ HI (Γ s ) can be obtained. Calculate/Estimate P LI i for All Tasks: For all the feasible values of β obtained in the last step, we can calculate P LI LO i for the tasks in Γ s . If Γ s contains all n tasks, we get a valid P LI DRMC and record the smallest value (lines 12 to 14). Otherwise, for other tasks in (Γ -Γ s ), assuming that each of them takes the next highest priority, we can also estimate their P LI LO i . If none of the result overall P LI DRMC from all the feasible values of β is less than the best known valid value, Γ s is pruned as it will lead to sub-optimal solutions (line 11). In this section, we illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed BBST-based heuristic through a case study and compare it against the solutions obtained from an Ipopt solver [1]. Here, we extract a small set of four tasks (two LC tasks τ 1 and τ 2 , and two HC tasks τ 3 and τ 4 ) from an automotive application [30], where their timing parameters are shown in Table III. Recall that the periods of HC tasks are fixed with p LO i = p HI i . For LC tasks, we consider two cases for the range of their periods with p max Recall that the periods of LC tasks in the HI running mode is set as p HI i = p max i to simplify the problem. That is, the problem becomes to find the feasible periods for LC tasks in the LO running mode as well as the priority assignment for all tasks in both LO and HI running modes to optimize the control performance of the tasks.

div.head: A. Equal Weight of LC and HC Tasks
div.p: As a first study, we consider the scenario where both LC and HC tasks have an equal contribution for the system control performance in the LO (normal) running mode. That is, we set a LO i = b LO i = 1 for all tasks (see Equation 19). The resulting period selection and priority assignment for the tasks as well as the achieved P LI DRMC from both the Ipopt solver [1] and BBST-based heuristic are shown in Table IV.

Note that, for the resulting tasks' priorities, smaller numbers indicate higher priorities. From the table, for the first case where there are p HI i = p max i = 2.5 • p min i for LC tasks, the BBST-based heuristic obtains slightly larger P LI DRMC when compared to the optimal result from the Ipopt solver (i.e., 257.04 vs. 246.50). It means that the solution from the BBSTbase heuristic can result in slightly worse control performance for the tasks in the LO running mode. This comes mainly due to the uniformly scaled low-level periods for LC tasks adopted in the BBST-based heuristic to simplify the problem. This limits its ability to find smaller periods for individual tasks as in the Ipopt solver. For instance, the period for task τ 1 is reduced from 38.54 to 37 in the solution of the Ipopt solver. However, it is worthwhile to note that the Ipopt solver takes more than 100 minutes to solve the problem while the BBST-based heuristic takes only a few milliseconds.

For the second case where LC tasks have p HI i = p max i = 3.0 • p min i , similar results are obtained and shown in the table as well. Here, we can see that, when LC tasks have larger high-level periods, the priority assignment for all tasks will change and better control performance for the tasks in the LO running mode can be achieved.

div.p: for LC tasks, we consider scenarios where HC tasks dominate system control performance. Specifically, when calculating P LI DRMC for tasks in the LO running mode, we reduce the the weight factors for LC tasks as a LO i = b LO i = 1/3 while keeping them as 1.0 for HC tasks. The resulting period and priority assignments for tasks are also shown in Table IV.

Here, we can see that, with the bias for HC tasks, both Ipopt solver and BBST-based heuristic will assign higher priorities to HC tasks (τ 3 and τ 4 ) in the LO running mode. Such priority assignment can effectively reduce R LO i for HC tasks and thus lead to better overall control performance. Moreover, with its flexibility of assigning periods for individual LC tasks, the Ipopt solver can increase the period p LO 2 of LC task τ 2 (from 18.5 to 27) which also help improve the worst-case response time of the HC task τ 4 in the LO running mode.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this work, for dual-criticality systems, we studied the schedulability analysis and performance optimization for dualrate mixed-criticality (DR-MC) tasks under the mode-switch fixed-priority (MS-FP) scheduler, where the periods of LC tasks and all tasks' priorities can change their at the modeswitch point to improve system schedulability. With mode transition being considered, we derived the schedulability condition for a set of DR-MC tasks under the MS-FP scheduler based on the response time analysis (RTA) technique. We also investigated how to select periods and priorities for tasks to optimize their control performance and formulate it as a Non-Linear Programming Optimization problem. Based on the Branch & Bound Search Tree (BBST) technique, we proposed an efficient heuristic for a simplified optimization problem. The effectiveness of the proposed BBST heuristic is illustrated through a case study.
